absent: Final teardown steps performed by deferred and direct release paths, including ordering with concurrent stack and RCU users.
Actual numeric values and layout widths for thread size, stack magic, capacity scale and flag bit positions.
Construction, balancing and teardown algorithms for scheduling domains and groups, including locking and lifetime rules.
Insertion, ordering and wakeup semantics of deferred wake queues and simple wait queues beyond the macros shown.
Conditions selecting between alternate task stack, accounting and virtual-time configurations and their runtime effects.
Error handling, failure modes and concurrency guarantees for user reference management and CPU topology queries.

findings.text: Task descriptor lifetime uses a usage counter. One helper unconditionally adds a reference and returns the same descriptor. Another helper adds a reference only when the count is already non-zero, returning the descriptor on success and a null indicator otherwise.

Releasing a task reference decrements the usage counter. If the counter remains non-zero the operation ends with no further action. If it reaches zero the final teardown is deferred through an RCU callback rather than executed inline, preserving safety under preemptive and blocking contexts.

A bulk release helper subtracts several references at once and invokes the final teardown directly when the count reaches zero. A scope cleanup binding ties the single-release helper to automatic invocation on scope exit when the pointer is non-null.
Thread teardown entry for a task descriptor is defined as having no observable effect in the routed configuration.
Architecture task descriptor size defaults to the full size of the task descriptor type.

A hardening helper reports a zero start offset and a length covering the region from the embedded thread member to the end of the task descriptor. Access to the task stack virtual memory descriptor either returns the stored descriptor or always returns null, depending on configuration.

Task stack location can be obtained from the stored stack pointer directly. One configuration provides a no-op thread stack setup and computes the stack end from the stack base with direction-dependent adjustment. Another configuration copies thread information between descriptors during setup and computes the stack end from thread information.

Stack pinning either conditionally acquires a stack reference and returns the stack location only on success, or unconditionally returns the stack location with a no-op release, depending on configuration.

Stack corruption is diagnosed by comparing the word at the stack end against a magic marker. Object containment checks whether an address after tag normalization lies within one thread stack extent anchored at the current stack base. A remaining-space query is defined to always report zero, and an end-of-stack address test uses alignment within thread size.
Scheduling domain flag debugging pairs metadata flags with a name. Domain attributes carry a single relaxation level, with a constructor initializing that level to a disabled sentinel.

Shared domain state holds reference and busy processor counts plus an idle-core indicator, a union selecting either an idle scan bound or allocation flags, and optionally utilization and capacity averages for cache-aware builds.

Scheduling domain descriptor links parent and child domains, balancing groups, timing bounds and tuning percentages, idle and flag state, load-balancing statistics and cost tracking, optional cache locality counters, optional detailed balancing statistics, a name, a construction-or-destruction union, shared state, and a span weight with out-of-line processor mask storage.

The processor span mask is not stored as an inline flexible member but as trailing storage immediately beyond the descriptor, sized at allocation to hold a full mask, avoiding overwrite by whole-structure initialization.

Per-processor scheduling data aggregates domain, group and capacity pointers. Topology levels combine a mask callback, a flags callback, a NUMA depth, embedded per-processor data and a name, with a constructor binding two callbacks and stringizing the name.

Default capacity scaling reports full scale, hardware pressure reports zero, hardware pressure update and energy rebuild and LLC byte update have no effect, frequency reference reports zero, and task NUMA node derives from the task processor.

Task CPU accounting groups system time, user time and total execution runtime. Per-user state groups a reference count, socket and pipe usage, hash linkage and identifier, conditional locked-memory accounting, conditional watch counts, and a rate-limit state.
User reference acquisition increments the internal count and returns the same object. A distinguished macro designates the initial privileged user object.

Deferred wake queue head stores a first node pointer and a tail link pointer. An empty queue is represented by a distinctive non-null sentinel in the first slot with the tail link pointing at the first slot, established by initializer, definition and init helpers, with an emptiness predicate testing for the sentinel.

Three unlock helpers pair preemption guarding with raw spin unlock, plain, interrupt-enabling, or flag-restoring respectively. Each optionally drains a deferred wake queue and reinitializes it after release, and each is annotated as releasing the passed lock.
Input and output accounting either accumulates read and write byte counts and increments read and write syscall counters in per-task storage, or is compiled to no effect, depending on configuration.

Simple wait queue head combines a raw spin lock with a task list. Queue entries pair a task pointer with list linkage. Static initializers bind an entry to the current task and initialize list and lock state.
Wait-queue occupancy is determined by list emptiness. Sleeper presence adds an ordering barrier before that test to synchronize with concurrent list insertion.

Exclusive wait macros share a prepare, test condition, handle interruptible signal, invoke a sleep action, and finalize cycle. Variants select uninterruptible, interruptible or idle sleep state, with or without timeout handling and timeout-adjusted condition evaluation, and skip sleeping entirely when the condition already holds.

User, guest and idle entry and exit notifications, reset and dynamic-tick start and stop, and interrupt and flush accounting are defined as having no effect in the routed configurations. Generic time accounting enablement queries delegate to context-tracking state, while one configuration always reports accounting enabled.
Guest entry and exit accounting bracket a kernel accounting step with setting and clearing of a virtual-CPU flag on the current task.
Each routed header defines a unique inclusion guard macro that marks the header as seen and prevents repeated inclusion.

During construction the shared scan bound storage temporarily holds allocation flags, so readers before the first periodic refresh may observe a small flag value as a relaxed scan bound; the value self-corrects on the first update.
A scoped guard constructor binds the task lock guard to a given task pointer for automatic acquisition and release.
Simple wait queue membership and wakeup coordination are serialized by the raw spin lock embedded in the queue head.
On-stack queue head declaration either initializes the head through the runtime initializer or uses static initialization, depending on configuration.

Scheduling domain flags are enumerated in two passes from a shared flag list: one pass assigns sequential positions with a count terminator, the other converts each position into a single-bit mask value.
Task creation and exit paths call into stack setup, stack location and thread teardown helpers with task descriptors to establish and release per-task execution state.
